published_item_inventory.title: Self-adjoint and normal endomorphisms of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space
In an orthonormal basis, self-adjoint means conjugate-transpose symmetry and normal means commuting with the conjugate transpose
If the characteristic polynomial of an endomorphism splits, some orthonormal basis makes its matrix upper triangular
A normal upper-triangular matrix is diagonal
Complex spectral theorem: a normal endomorphism of a finite-dimensional complex inner product space has an orthonormal eigenbasis, and conversely
A real normal endomorphism is orthogonally block-diagonalisable with 1x1 real blocks and 2x2 rotation-scaling blocks
Real spectral theorem: a self-adjoint endomorphism of a finite-dimensional real inner product space has an orthonormal eigenbasis
A normal endomorphism is a sum of its eigenvalues times pairwise orthogonal projections, and each spectral projection is a polynomial in the endomorphism
The spectral functional calculus f(T) for a normal endomorphism
For normal endomorphisms, the spectral functional calculus respects sums, products, adjoints, and composition of scalar functions
Semisimple endomorphisms as endomorphisms diagonalisable over an algebraic closure, and nilpotent endomorphisms
Over a perfect field, every endomorphism has a unique commuting semisimple-plus-nilpotent decomposition, polynomial in the endomorphism
Non-negative and positive operators
Over the reals, non-negative and positive operators correspond exactly to positive semidefinite and positive definite symmetric forms
A non-negative operator is equivalently self-adjoint with nonnegative eigenvalues, a positive semidefinite matrix in an orthonormal basis, or an operator of the form S^*S
A non-negative operator has a unique non-negative square root
The non-negative square root of a non-negative operator is a polynomial in the operator
The singular values of a linear map as the eigenvalues of the positive square root of T^*T
Singular values are well defined because the positive square root of T^*T is unique
Every linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces admits a singular value decomposition
The rank of a linear map is the number of its nonzero singular values
An endomorphism and its adjoint have the same singular values
Every endomorphism has a polar decomposition T = SU with U non-negative and S an isometry on the orthogonal complement of ker T, and S is unique exactly when T is invertible
The operator norm is zero on the zero domain and otherwise is max_{||v||=1} ||Tv||
The operator norm is 0 on the zero domain and otherwise equals the largest singular value, attained at a right-singular vector
The operator norm is submultiplicative and satisfies ||T^*T|| = ||T||^2
The best rank-at-most-k approximation in operator norm is the rank-k truncation of a singular value decomposition
The Rayleigh quotient of a nonzero vector for a self-adjoint endomorphism
Courant-Fischer min-max principle for self-adjoint endomorphisms on finite-dimensional real inner product spaces
The smallest and largest eigenvalues of a self-adjoint endomorphism are the minimum and maximum Rayleigh quotients
The eigenvalues of the orthogonal compression of a self-adjoint endomorphism to a hyperplane interlace those of the original endomorphism
Weyl inequalities bound the eigenvalues of a sum of self-adjoint endomorphisms
The Gershgorin disks of an endomorphism with respect to an ordered basis
Every eigenvalue lies in some Gershgorin disk
Absolute and relative forward error for an approximate value of a problem map
Absolute and relative local condition numbers of a problem map
The matrix norm induced by a published vector p-norm
Induced matrix norms are compatible with matrix-vector multiplication, submultiplicative, and satisfy ||I|| = 1
The induced 1-norm is the maximum column sum and the induced infinity-norm is the maximum row sum
The Frobenius norm $\lVert A\rVert_F=(\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^2)^{1/2}$ on real or complex matrices
Spectral and Frobenius norms are unitarily invariant, are given by singular values, and satisfy the sharp rank comparison
The condition number kappa_p(A) = ||A||_p ||A^{-1}||_p of a nonsingular linear system
Right-hand-side perturbations in Ax = b are amplified by the condition number
Matrix perturbations in Ax = b obey a first-order condition-number bound
The reciprocal spectral condition number is the relative distance to singularity
Residual bounds on forward error for a nonsingular linear system
Normwise and componentwise backward error for an approximate linear-system solution
Residual formulas for normwise and componentwise backward error
The standard relative floating-point model and unit roundoff
Forward and backward stability for a problem family under an arithmetic model
If |delta_i| <= u and n u < 1, then prod (1+delta_i) = 1 + theta_n with |theta_n| <= gamma_n
The computed floating-point dot product obeys componentwise and normwise error bounds
Local conditioning times backward error controls forward error to first order
For full-column-rank A, the normal equations square the spectral condition number
Exact rank is locally constant at full-rank matrices and discontinuous at nonmaximal-rank matrices
Numerical rank relative to a declared norm, scale, and tolerance
In the spectral norm, numerical rank counts the singular values above the declared threshold
Forward and backward substitution for triangular linear systems
Forward and backward substitution are correct, unique, and quadratic in scalar operations
A normalised LU factorisation has a unit lower-triangular L and an upper-triangular U
An LDU factorisation has unit lower-triangular L, diagonal D, and unit upper-triangular U
Normalised LU and LDU factorisations with nonzero pivots are unique
Block LU factorisation and the associated Schur complement
An invertible leading block yields block LU through its Schur complement
A square matrix has an unpivoted unit-lower LU factorisation exactly when all leading principal minors are nonzero
When unpivoted elimination runs to completion, the elimination multipliers are the entries of the normalised LU factors
Permutation matrices, partial pivoting, and the pivot-growth factor
Every real or complex square matrix admits a PLU factorisation, and the first failed pivot marks the singular boundary
In the standard real floating-point model, computed pivoted LU is a nearby factorisation with a pivot-growth dependent backward bound
Hermitian positive-definite matrices and Cholesky factorisation A = LL* with positive diagonal
A matrix admits a Cholesky factorisation with positive diagonal exactly when it is Hermitian positive definite, and that factor is unique
For real symmetric matrices, positive leading principal minors are equivalent to positive Cholesky pivots
Cholesky solves Hermitian positive-definite systems and has about half the factorisation cost of LU
Householder reflectors in real or complex inner-product spaces
Real Givens rotations and complex Givens transformations
Householder reflectors and Givens transformations are unitary and can annihilate prescribed entries
Full, reduced, and column-pivoted computational QR factorisations
Successive Householder or Givens transformations produce full and reduced QR factorisations with the standard dense operation counts
A local Householder backward-error bound yields a backward-stable QR factorisation
Exact column-pivoted QR of a real or complex rank-r matrix has an invertible leading triangular block and zero trailing block
Reduced QR over the reals solves full-column-rank least squares without squaring the condition number
The Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse $A^+$ as the solution of the four Penrose equations
Every finite real or complex matrix has a unique Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse
Pseudoinversion is involutive, commutes with adjoints, and is equivariant under unitary left and right factors
$AA^+$ and $A^+A$ are the orthogonal projections onto $\operatorname{im}A$ and $\operatorname{im}A^*$
The Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse exchanges image and adjoint-image, and exchanges kernel and adjoint-kernel
If $A$ has full column rank, then $A^+=(A^*A)^{-1}A^*$
If $A$ has full row rank, then $A^+=A^*(AA^*)^{-1}$
For every right-hand side $b$, $A^+b$ is the unique least-squares solution of minimum Euclidean norm
Every least-squares solution has the form $A^+b+(I-A^+A)z$, and the same affine family specializes to exact solutions when $b\in\operatorname{im}A$
Reduced QR gives the full-column and full-row-rank pseudoinverse formulas without forming normal equations
The Tikhonov regularised least-squares objective $\|Ax-b\|_2^2+\lambda\|x\|_2^2$ for $\lambda>0$
For every $\lambda>0$, the Tikhonov objective is strictly convex and has the unique minimiser $(A^*A+\lambda I)^{-1}A^*b$
Tikhonov regularisation scales each singular component by the filter factor $\sigma/(\sigma^2+\lambda)$
As $\lambda\downarrow0$, the Tikhonov minimisers converge to the Moore--Penrose solution $A^+b$
The truncated singular-value pseudoinverse obtained by discarding singular values below a declared numerical-rank threshold
Truncated SVD and Tikhonov regularisation act as hard and smooth spectral filters on the singular components
The Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse is continuous on each fixed-rank stratum and is not continuous across rank loss
The residual $r=Ax-\mu x$ and the normwise backward error of an approximate eigenpair
For a unit vector $x$, the smallest perturbation making $(\mu,x)$ an exact eigenpair has spectral norm $\|Ax-\mu x\|_2$
Power iteration with normalisation and Rayleigh-quotient eigenvalue estimates

If a diagonalisable matrix has a simple eigenvalue of strictly largest modulus and the start vector has a nonzero component in that eigendirection, power iteration converges projectively at the eigenvalue-ratio rate
Inverse iteration and shifted inverse iteration
If $\mu$ is not an eigenvalue and one simple eigenvalue is uniquely nearest to $\mu$, shifted inverse iteration converges to its eigendirection
Rayleigh-quotient iteration for Hermitian matrices
For a Hermitian matrix, the eigenvectors are the stationary points of the Rayleigh quotient and twice the residual is its constrained gradient
For Hermitian matrices, the Rayleigh quotient and residual converge with the expected rates along power iteration
Near a simple Hermitian eigenvector, Rayleigh-quotient iteration converges cubically
Subspace iteration and the dominant invariant subspace of a matrix
Subspace iteration converges to the dominant invariant subspace when a spectral gap separates the wanted and unwanted eigenvalues
Upper Hessenberg matrices and real symmetric tridiagonal matrices
Householder similarities reduce a general matrix to upper Hessenberg form and a real symmetric matrix to tridiagonal form
Unshifted QR iteration, shifted QR iteration, deflation, and the Wilkinson shift
Unshifted QR is orthonormalised simultaneous iteration, and every QR iterate is unitarily similar to the original matrix
Under separated moduli and leading-minor hypotheses, unshifted QR drives the strict lower triangle to zero and orders the eigenvalues on the diagonal
Shifted QR iteration preserves upper Hessenberg form
A real Wilkinson-shifted symmetric tridiagonal QR step preserves symmetric tridiagonal form away from ties
A residual threshold on a normalised approximate eigenpair is exactly a normwise backward-error stopping rule

claim_coverage.contract: Exact arithmetic. Normal/self-adjoint hypotheses are explicit; SVD exists for every finite-dimensional map. Local SVD existence proof is included.
Conditional on the standard relative model and each relevant operation remaining in the normal range; overflow, underflow, and invalid operations are excluded.

Exact LU hypotheses distinguish no-pivot leading-minor criteria from PLU existence. Floating-point GEPP has an entrywise and normwise backward bound proportional to the pivot-growth factor; no dimension-independent growth guarantee is asserted.

Exact existence iff Hermitian positive definite, positive diagonal convention, uniqueness, solve by triangular substitutions, dense factorization cost ~n^3/3. No local floating-point backward-error theorem or explicit recurrence is presently on this page.

Exact QR construction and operation counts are proved; exact reduced-QR least-squares solve requires full column rank. The published Householder QR backward-error theorem assumes a local computed-step perturbation bound [A1], which is not proved from the standard model in that item.

claim_coverage.topic: General least squares, SVD, and pseudoinverse
claim_coverage.contract: Exact arithmetic; the SVD theorem is a mathematical existence theorem, not a numerical SVD procedure. Regularized and truncated filters have local statements and proofs.

Residual gives exact minimum normwise matrix backward error for a unit vector. Iteration convergence claims are exact-arithmetic and require their stated simplicity, spectral-gap, and leading-minor/tie conditions; no finite-precision QR eigenvalue stability theorem is included in these pages.

scope_findings: The exact mathematical content required for conditioning, error vocabulary, LU/PLU, Cholesky existence/solve/cost, QR, least squares, pseudoinverse, SVD existence, spectral theory, and exact-arithmetic eigenvalue iteration already has published local suppliers.
Numerical analysis-specific arithmetic claims must preserve the floating-point model exclusions and dimension/range assumptions carried by their local statements.
The local matrix-norms page is the canonical provider for condition numbers, residuals and backward-error vocabulary; do not redeclare these contracts in a Numerical Analysis page.
The local direct-factorization page is the canonical provider for LU/PLU, Cholesky, Householder/Givens QR, triangular solves, and their exact operation counts.
The local pseudoinverse page is the canonical provider for minimum-norm least squares, rank-deficient least squares, regularization, and spectral filters.
The local spectral and eigen-iteration pages are exact-arithmetic suppliers. Their existence and convergence claims do not by themselves assert a floating-point SVD or eigenvalue algorithm.
